method_card.title: Scatter Diagrams, Population Pyramids and Choropleth Maps
method_card.content:
A scatter diagram plots pairs of values (bivariate data) to show the relationship between two variables. The pattern of the points indicates the type and strength of correlation: positive correlation (both variables increase together), negative correlation (one increases as the other decreases), or no correlation (no pattern). Strength is described as strong, moderate or weak depending on how closely the points cluster around a straight line.

Critical rule: correlation does not imply causation. Even a very strong correlation does not mean one variable causes the other — there may be a confounding variable, or the relationship may be coincidental.

A line of best fit is drawn through the mean point \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\) to minimise the overall distance of points from the line. Use it to estimate values within the data range (interpolation). Estimating outside the data range is extrapolation and is unreliable.

A population pyramid is a back-to-back horizontal bar chart showing the age and gender structure of a population. The left bars show males, the right show females. Each horizontal bar represents an age group. Compare two pyramids by commenting on the shape (wide base = young population; wide top = ageing population), the relative sizes of male and female bars, and the overall size.

A choropleth map uses shading (or colour intensity) to represent data values for geographic regions. Darker shading typically represents higher values. To read a choropleth map: identify the key, note which shading category a region falls into, and read the corresponding data range. Students will not be expected to draw these in the exam — only to read and interpret them.
steps: Describe correlation by direction (positive/negative/none) and strength (strong/moderate/weak)
Never claim causation from correlation alone — state correlation only
To use a line of best fit, find the x-value on the horizontal axis, draw a vertical line up to the line, then read across to the y-axis
State whether an estimate is interpolation (within the data range — more reliable) or extrapolation (outside — less reliable)
For population pyramids, compare the age group with the widest bar and describe overall shape
For choropleth maps, use the key to identify the shading category and read the data range

exam_context.marks: 2–5 marks; correlation identification is 1 mark; reading from line of best fit is 1–2 marks; population pyramid comparison is 3–4 marks; choropleth map interpretation is 1–2 marks
exam_context.frequency: Scatter diagrams appear on virtually every paper; population pyramid comparison and choropleth map interpretation appear on roughly two-thirds of papers

worked_examples.question: A scatter diagram shows the hours of sunshine and the number of ice cream sales on 8 days. As hours of sunshine increase, ice cream sales also increase. What type of correlation is shown?

steps.label: Step 1 — Identify the pattern
steps.content: Both variables increase together: as sunshine increases, sales increase.

steps.label: Step 2 — Name the correlation
steps.content: When both variables increase together, this is positive correlation.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Positive correlation. As hours of sunshine increase, ice cream sales increase.

worked_examples.question: A line of best fit on a scatter diagram passes through the points (2, 14) and (8, 26). Estimate the y-value when x = 5.

steps.label: Step 1 — Find the gradient of the line of best fit
Answer
steps.content: When x = 5, the estimated y-value is 20. This is interpolation (x = 5 is within the data range 2 to 8), so the estimate is reliable.

worked_examples.question: Two population pyramids are shown for Country A and Country B. Country A has wide bars at ages 0–14 and narrow bars at ages 65+. Country B has roughly equal bar widths across all age groups with slightly wider bars at 45–64. Compare the two populations in context.

steps.label: Step 1 — Describe Country A's structure
steps.content: Country A's pyramid is wide at the base (young population, many children aged 0–14) and narrow at the top (few elderly people). This is a rapidly growing population typical of a less economically developed country.

steps.label: Step 2 — Describe Country B's structure
steps.content: Country B has a more uniform distribution across age groups with a slight bulge at 45–64, suggesting an ageing population with low birth rates and high life expectancy. This is typical of a more economically developed country.

steps.label: Step 3 — Compare in context
steps.content: Country A has a higher proportion of young dependants; Country B has a higher proportion of older people near or in retirement. Country B faces greater pressure on pension and healthcare systems; Country A faces pressure on schools and employment growth.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Country A has a young, growing population (wide base); Country B has an ageing population (uniform or top-heavy pyramid). They face different demographic challenges: Country A needs to expand education and employment, while Country B needs to support an ageing population.

bronze.display: A scatter diagram shows that as a car's age increases, its value decreases. What type of correlation is this?
options: Positive correlation
Negative correlation
No correlation
Perfect correlation

misconceptions.message: When one variable increases and the other decreases, this is negative correlation. The word 'negative' refers to the direction, not to the quality of the relationship.

bronze.display: A scatter diagram shows points roughly following a line from bottom-left to top-right, with some scatter around the line. What is the best description?
options: Strong negative correlation
No correlation
Moderate positive correlation
Perfect positive correlation

misconceptions.message: Bottom-left to top-right = positive direction. Points not tightly clustered = moderate strength. 'Perfect' correlation means all points exactly on a line — here there is scatter.

bronze.display: A choropleth map uses shading to show average household income. The key shows: light grey = £20,000–£30,000; medium grey = £30,000–£40,000; dark grey = £40,000–£50,000. A region shaded medium grey has an average income in which range?
options: Cannot tell from the map alone

misconceptions.message: Always read the choropleth key. Medium grey is defined in the key as £30,000–£40,000. Do not assume the darkest shade always means the highest value — check the key.

bronze.display: A population pyramid shows Country X with wide bars at age groups 0–14 and narrow bars at 60+. What does this suggest about Country X's population?
options: An ageing population with low birth rates
A young, growing population with high birth rates
A stable population with equal numbers at all ages
A declining population with more elderly than young

misconceptions.message: A wide base (ages 0–14) means many young people = high birth rate = growing population. A narrow top means fewer elderly, suggesting either lower life expectancy or a younger population overall.

bronze.display: A line of best fit passes through (0, 5) and (10, 25). What is the gradient of the line?
A scatter diagram plots hours of TV watched per day against exam score for 20 students. The points form a clear downward slope from left to right. What can be concluded?
options: Watching more TV causes lower exam scores
There is a negative correlation between TV hours and exam scores
Students who watch no TV always achieve the highest scores
There is a positive correlation between TV hours and exam scores

misconceptions.message: A downward slope shows negative correlation — as TV hours increase, scores tend to decrease. This does NOT prove causation. Never say 'watching TV causes lower scores' from a scatter diagram alone.

bronze.display: Two population pyramids are shown. Pyramid A has bars that are much wider on the left (male) side than the right (female) side across all age groups. What does this suggest?
options: There are significantly more males than females in the population
The female population is older on average
The male birth rate is lower than the female birth rate
Both populations are equal in size

misconceptions.message: Left bars = males; right bars = females. Consistently wider left bars means more males than females across all age groups.

bronze.display: A line of best fit on a scatter diagram has equation y = 3x + 7. Estimate y when x = 4.

silver.display: A line of best fit passes through the mean point (5, 18) and also through (9, 30). Estimate y when x = 7.

A scatter diagram for 12 data points shows hours of sunlight (x, range 3–10) and crop yield (y, tonnes). The line of best fit has equation y = 0.8x + 2. A farmer wants to estimate yield when x = 15 hours. Is this estimate reliable?
options: Yes — the line of best fit can always be extended
No — x = 15 is outside the data range (3–10), making this extrapolation, which is unreliable
Yes — a strong positive correlation makes extrapolation accurate
No — the equation cannot be used for predictions at all

misconceptions.message: x = 15 lies outside the observed data range of 3–10. Extending the line beyond the data is extrapolation, which is less reliable because the relationship may not continue in the same way.

silver.display: Two population pyramids are compared. Country P has a broad base (ages 0–4: 18%; 5–14: 22%) and Country Q has a narrow base (ages 0–4: 6%; 5–14: 9%). Which country has the higher proportion of under-15s?
options: Country Q (15%)
Country P (40%)
Both countries have the same proportion of under-15s
Cannot tell from the data given

misconceptions.message: Country P under-15s: 18 + 22 = 40%. Country Q under-15s: 6 + 9 = 15%. Country P has a much younger population profile.

silver.display: A choropleth map shows regional unemployment rates with 4 shading bands: 0–5%: white; 5–10%: light grey; 10–15%: dark grey; 15%+: black. A journalist says 'the darkest region has unemployment exactly three times the lightest region.' Is this necessarily correct?
options: Yes — 15% is exactly three times 5%
No — the darkest region is 15%+ (could be 20%), and the lightest region could be any value from 0–5%
Yes — choropleth maps always show exact values
No — the lightest shading always means zero unemployment

misconceptions.message: Choropleth maps show a range, not an exact value. The darkest region has at least 15% but could be much higher. The lightest region has 0–5%. You cannot compare exact values from shading alone.

silver.display: A scatter diagram shows a strong negative correlation between price (£) and number of units sold for 10 products. The line of best fit has equation y = −2.5x + 120, where x is price and y is units sold. Estimate units sold when price = 30.

A student says: 'The scatter diagram shows a strong positive correlation between shoe size and reading age. Therefore, having larger feet improves your ability to read.' What is wrong with this conclusion?
options: Nothing — strong correlation always implies causation
Correlation does not imply causation; both shoe size and reading age increase with the child's age (confounding variable)
The correlation is clearly not positive, so the whole statement is wrong
Causation can only be concluded from negative correlation, not positive

misconceptions.message: Even a very strong correlation does not establish cause and effect. Here, the confounding variable is the child's age: as children get older, both feet and reading ability develop — larger feet don't cause better reading.

gold.display: A scatter diagram has 12 data points with x values ranging from 5 to 25. The mean point is (15, 42). The line of best fit also passes through (5, 22). Write the equation of the line of best fit in the form y = mx + c.

misconceptions.message: Gradient m = (42−22)/(15−5) = 20/10 = 2. Using point (5,22): c = 22 − 2(5) = 12. Equation: y = 2x + 12. Verify with mean point: y = 2(15)+12 = 42. Correct.

gold.display: Two population pyramids compare a city in 2000 and 2025. In 2000, the 0–14 age group was the largest; in 2025, the 45–64 age group is the largest and the 0–14 group has shrunk. What demographic change does this suggest?
options: The population is getting younger due to increased birth rates
The population has aged over 25 years, with falling birth rates and increasing life expectancy
The city has seen a large influx of young migrants
The population size has remained constant but the age structure is unchanged

misconceptions.message: A shift in the largest age group from 0–14 to 45–64 over 25 years shows the same generation ageing through the pyramid, combined with a shrinking base (fewer births). This is demographic ageing.

gold.display: A scatter diagram plots revision hours (x, range 0–12) against exam marks (y, range 20–95) for 20 students. The correlation is positive and moderate. A student revised for 14 hours. A teacher uses the line of best fit to predict the mark as 102. Explain why this prediction is problematic.
options: 14 hours of revision always guarantees full marks, so 102 is an underestimate
x = 14 is outside the observed data range (0–12), making this extrapolation. Also, marks are capped at 100, so 102 is impossible.
The correlation is only moderate so no prediction can ever be made
Lines of best fit cannot produce values above the mean y-value

misconceptions.message: Two separate problems: (1) x = 14 is beyond the data range — extrapolation is unreliable. (2) Exam marks are bounded at 100, so a predicted value of 102 is impossible regardless of the equation.

gold.display: A choropleth map shows life expectancy by region. Region A is shaded in the highest band (75–80 years) and Region B is in the second band (70–75 years). A student claims Region A residents live on average 10 years longer than Region B residents. Is this correct?
options: Yes — the bands are 5 years apart so 10 years is correct
No — the actual difference could be as small as 0 years or as large as 10 years, but the shading bands only confirm the ranges, not exact values
No — choropleth maps cannot compare two regions
Yes — darker shading always means a larger value

misconceptions.message: Region A is 75–80 years; Region B is 70–75 years. If A = 75.1 and B = 74.9, the difference is only 0.2 years. If A = 80 and B = 70, the difference is 10 years. The shading gives a range, not an exact value, so the actual difference is unknown from shading alone.

gold.display: A scatter diagram plots the number of doctors per 1,000 people (x) and infant mortality rate per 1,000 births (y) for 15 countries. There is a strong negative correlation. A journalist writes: 'Countries with more doctors have lower infant mortality — this proves that increasing the number of doctors reduces infant deaths.' Evaluate this conclusion.
options: The conclusion is fully supported — strong negative correlation is enough to establish causation
The conclusion is partly right — more doctors correlates with lower mortality, but this could reflect overall wealth (a confounding variable), not a direct causal link
The conclusion is wrong because the correlation is negative, which means the variables are unrelated
The conclusion is correct because the journalist has used the word 'proves', which implies a statistical test

misconceptions.message: Strong negative correlation does suggest a meaningful relationship, but wealthier countries tend to have both more doctors AND lower infant mortality — wealth is a confounding variable. The scatter diagram alone cannot distinguish the direct effect of doctors from the indirect effect of national wealth.
